title: Deep litter management in a poultry house
subtitle: Building a living floor that composts in place and reduces disease pressure.
excerpt: Deep litter is a management system in which bedding material is added on top of existing litter rather than removed, allowing it to compost in place on the house floor. A correctly managed deep litter bed stays warm, dry, and low-ammonia through the winter and produces usable compost by spring. A poorly managed one becomes a wet, ammonia-heavy disease reservoir.
sourceNotes: AHDB Poultry, housed flock management guidance. University of Nebraska Extension, Deep Litter Systems for Poultry. RSPCA Farm Animal Welfare guidance on floor housing.

glossaryTerms.definition: A bedding management system in which successive layers of dry material (straw, wood shavings, or a mix) are added on top of existing manure-saturated bedding. Microbial activity composts the lower layers in place, generating heat and destroying some pathogens.

content.text: bed is not accumulated filth. It is an actively composting floor. The key is carbon: each time the bed becomes wet or compacted on the surface, a new layer of dry, carbon-rich material is added on top. The ratio of carbon to nitrogen stays above 25:1, the ammonia stays bound, and the microbial heat keeps the flock warm and the pathogens suppressed.
Start with a clean, dry floor. Lay a 15 cm base of wood shavings, chopped straw, or a 50:50 mix.
Introduce birds. For the first two weeks, check the surface daily for wet patches. Any wet area should be removed and replaced with dry material.
After the initial two weeks, add a 5 cm layer of dry material on top of the existing bed each month, or whenever the surface looks damp or compacted.
Turn the top 10 cm with a fork once a week. This aerates the bed, prevents caking, and encourages the birds to scratch.
Keep water drinkers raised off the floor on a slatted platform or outside the house. Spilled water is the biggest risk to a deep litter bed.
Watch ammonia levels. If you smell a sharp, eye-watering ammonia when you open the house door in the morning, the nitrogen-to-carbon ratio is off. Add dry straw or shavings and turn the bed.
A well-managed bed has no ammonia smell, a slight warmth when you push your hand in, and a crumbly surface texture.

The bed is cleared once a year, usually in spring when outdoor access improves. A fully composted deep litter bed at clearout is dark, crumbly, low-odour, and an excellent garden amendment. Spread it on the vegetable plot and dig it in. Allow the house to dry for a week before starting a fresh bed.

A wet, slimy bed with a strong ammonia smell has failed. Strip it out entirely, allow the floor to dry, and address the source of moisture (drinker leaks, roof drips, or condensation from overcrowding) before starting again. Continuing to add dry material to a failed wet bed will not save it.
